displayQuote: The test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposed ideas in mind at the same time

meta.title: Who really said "The test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposed ideas in mind at the same time"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: F. Scott Fitzgerald wrote this in his 1936 Esquire essay "The Crack-Up" — though his original line says "in the mind," not "in mind."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposed ideas in mind at the same time'?
meta.ogDescription: Traced to F. Scott Fitzgerald's 1936 essay "The Crack-Up" — with one small word quietly dropped along the way.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Fitzgerald’s confessional essay “The Crack-Up,” first published in Esquire magazine in February 1936. His exact sentence reads “the ability to hold two opposed ideas in the mind at the same time, and still retain the ability to function” — the popular version quoted here has quietly dropped the word “the.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Crack-Up (New Directions, 1945, ed. Edmund Wilson)

source.excerpt: Before I go on with this short history, let me make a general observation—the test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposed ideas in the mind at the same time, and still retain the ability to function. One should, for example, be able to see that things are hopeless and yet be determined to make them otherwise.
trail: First published in Esquire magazine, February 1936, as the opening piece of a three-part series — followed by “Pasting It Together” (March 1936) and “Handle with Care” (April 1936), as documented in Wikipedia’s entry on The Crack-Up ↗.
Collected the following decade in The Crack-Up (New Directions, 1945) ↗, edited by Fitzgerald’s friend Edmund Wilson.

The exact passage, including the closing clause of the same sentence about “the ability to function,” is documented by Quote Investigator ↗, which also traces how the wording drifted in later popular use.
source.excerptNote: The commonly quoted version trims “the” before “mind” and is often cut off before Fitzgerald’s actual point — retaining the ability to function.

source.rightsHolder: Estate of F. Scott Fitzgerald, published by New Directions Publishing Corp.
source.rightsNote: The copyright is actively held and exercised: the essay is still commercially published in the 1945 collection by New Directions Publishing ↗, and the PBS reprint of the excerpt carries the line “This excerpt is reprinted with the permission of New Directions Publishing.” The 1936 publication date alone would not settle it — U.S. works published between 1929 and 1963 entered the public domain unless copyright was renewed in the 28th year — so we rely on the live, exercised claim rather than the date.

author.name: F. Scott Fitzgerald
author.heading: About F. Scott Fitzgerald
author.metaLine: 1896–1940 · American novelist & essayist, author of The Great Gatsby
author.bio: Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was a leading voice of the American “Jazz Age,” best known for the 1925 novel The Great Gatsby. In the mid-1930s, financially strained and in declining health, he wrote a series of unusually candid personal essays for Esquire chronicling his psychological breakdown, later collected as The Crack-Up.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The authorship here is not in question — but the wording that circulates online has drifted from what Fitzgerald actually wrote.

items.who: Popular quotation sites and social media
items.why: Widely reproduce the line as “hold two opposed ideas in mind” and often stop there, whereas Fitzgerald’s original reads “in the mind at the same time, and still retain the ability to function” — a clause that carries his actual point. Quote Investigator ↗ documents the original 1936 wording and how the phrasing evolved over time.

misattribution.truthLine: Fitzgerald genuinely wrote this sentence, in his 1936 essay “The Crack-Up” ↗; the version quoted around the internet is simply a lightly trimmed paraphrase of his own words, not a fabrication or a misattribution to the wrong author.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Fitzgerald wrote “The Crack-Up” during one of the lowest points of his life — broke, drinking heavily, and watching his once-celebrated career stall while his wife Zelda was institutionalized. The essay was startlingly candid for its time: a famous novelist publicly admitting psychological collapse, at a moment when such confessions were rare in American letters.

The line about “first-rate intelligence” appears early in the essay as a general observation before Fitzgerald turns to his own story, describing how he had once been able to hold contradictory beliefs — seeing life as both futile and worth striving in — without being paralyzed by the contradiction.
context.pull: One should be able to see that things are hopeless and yet be determined to make them otherwise.
